blocks.text: A 22-year-old falls on her outstretched hand while skating. Her wrist is tender in the hollow at the base of the thumb, but the first X-ray looks normal. A fracture of the scaphoid is exactly the injury that hides on early films, and the anatomy of the carpus explains both why it is common and why it can go wrong.

blocks.markdown: The distal upper limb has three jobs: position the hand in space (elbow and forearm), transmit force to it (wrist), and use it for grip and fine manipulation (hand). In this unit we cover the joints and movements of the elbow and forearm, the carpal bones, and the muscles behind the two classic types of grip.

blocks.title: Elbow and radioulnar joints
blocks.text: The elbow joint is a synovial hinge joint between the humerus and both forearm bones (humeroulnar and humeroradial articulations). It allows flexion and extension only. Pronation and supination of the forearm occur at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints (both pivot joints), where the radius rotates around the ulna.

rows: Supinator; biceps brachii (powerful when the elbow is flexed)
blocks.caption: Movements of the elbow and forearm.

blocks.markdown: **Pronation and supination.** In supination the radius and ulna lie parallel; in pronation the distal radius crosses over the ulna. The movement is rotation of the radius around an axis running from the radial head at the elbow to the ulnar head at the wrist. The radial head is held against the ulna by the **annular ligament**. In young children (typically under about five years) a sudden pull on the extended, pronated arm can slip the radial head under the lower edge of the annular ligament, producing a 'pulled elbow' (subluxation of the radial head): the child will not use the arm and holds it still, in pronation.

blocks.title: Which muscle supinates the flexed forearm?
blocks.prompt: You are asked to turn a screw with the elbow flexed to 90 degrees and the palm up. Which muscle gives most of the force, and which muscle can supinate when the elbow is fully extended?

steps.text: Supination is produced by the supinator and by biceps brachii. Biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity and, when the forearm is pronated, pulls to rotate the radius back.
Biceps is also an elbow flexor, so it is most effective at supination when the elbow is flexed.
With the elbow extended, biceps is less well placed, so supinator, which acts regardless of elbow position, does the work.

blocks.answer: Biceps brachii is the main supinator when the elbow is flexed; supinator acts at any elbow position and is the main supinator when the elbow is extended.

blocks.markdown: **The carpal bones.** Eight carpal bones lie in two rows. From lateral (radial) to medial (ulnar), the **proximal row** is **scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform**; the **distal row** is **trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate**. The scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum articulate with the radius (and an articular disc) at the radiocarpal joint; the pisiform is a sesamoid bone within the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and sits on the front of the triquetrum. A common mnemonic is 'Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle'.

blocks.title: Scaphoid: the most commonly fractured carpal bone
blocks.text: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, usually from a fall on the outstretched hand (FOOSH). Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox (between the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis laterally and extensor pollicis longus medially) is the classic sign. The blood supply, mainly from branches of the radial artery, enters the bone distally and runs retrograde to the proximal pole. A fracture through the waist can therefore cut off the supply to the proximal fragment, causing avascular necrosis and non-union. Early radiographs may appear normal, so suspected scaphoid fractures are immobilised and re-imaged or investigated further.

rows: Scaphoid fractures are most common; the lunate can dislocate anteriorly into the carpal tunnel
Trapezium forms the saddle joint of the thumb (first carpometacarpal joint); hamulus (hook) of hamate can fracture
blocks.caption: The carpal bones.

blocks.markdown: **Grips.** The hand has two main types of grip. In a **power grip** (for example gripping a hammer or a bar) the fingers flex around the object, the thumb lies across it, and the wrist is held in extension. The long flexors of the fingers (**flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus**) and **flexor pollicis longus** provide the force, and the wrist extensors (**extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris**) set the wrist in extension so the flexor tendons work at an effective length. A **precision grip** (for example threading a needle or holding a pen) uses the fingertips and thumb pad, and depends on the **intrinsic muscles**: the **lumbricals**, the **dorsal interossei** (abduct the fingers, DAB), the **palmar interossei** (adduct the fingers, PAD), and the **thenar muscles** (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis) with adductor pollicis.

rows: Flexor digitorum profundus and superficialis, flexor pollicis longus; wrist extensors
Lumbricals, interossei, thenar muscles, adductor pollicis
Mainly ulnar; median for thenar muscles and lateral two lumbricals
blocks.caption: Power versus precision grip. The thenar muscles are median nerve (recurrent branch), most other intrinsic muscles ulnar.

blocks.title: Why does the wrist extend during a strong grip?
blocks.prompt: Explain why a person making a tight fist automatically extends the wrist.

steps.text: The long finger flexors cross the wrist, so when they contract they also tend to flex the wrist.
If the wrist flexed, the flexor tendons would shorten and lose force (active insufficiency).
The wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris) contract to hold the wrist in slight extension, keeping the flexor muscles at a good working length.

blocks.answer: The wrist extensors fix the wrist so that the long finger flexors can exert maximum force.

blocks.title: Do not forget the pivot
blocks.text: Pronation and supination do not occur at the elbow joint itself. A patient may flex and extend the elbow normally with a dislocated or damaged radioulnar joint; the forearm rotation is the part that is lost. Test the movements separately.

points: The elbow is a hinge joint (flexion and extension); pronation and supination happen at the proximal and distal radioulnar pivot joints.

Carpals from lateral to medial: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform (proximal); trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate (distal). The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured, with a risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
Power grip uses the long finger flexors with the wrist extensors; precision grip relies on the intrinsic hand muscles (lumbricals, interossei, thenar muscles, adductor pollicis).

questions.stem: Which movements occur at the elbow joint itself?

distractorRationale.b: Pronation and supination occur at the radioulnar joints.
distractorRationale.c: The elbow is a hinge joint and does not abduct or adduct.
distractorRationale.d: Circumduction is a movement of ball-and-socket joints such as the shoulder.

questions.explanation: The elbow is a hinge joint, which limits movement to flexion and extension about one transverse axis. Forearm rotation takes place at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints.

questions.stem: Which carpal bone is the most lateral bone in the proximal row?

distractorRationale.b: The lunate lies medial to the scaphoid.
distractorRationale.c: The capitate is in the distal row.
distractorRationale.d: The hamate is in the distal row, on the ulnar side.

questions.explanation: The proximal row runs from lateral to medial as scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. The scaphoid is therefore the most lateral, directly beneath the anatomical snuffbox.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old falls on her outstretched hand and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. The first radiograph is normal. Why is a fracture of the scaphoid waist still a concern?

options.text: The proximal fragment has a retrograde blood supply and may become avascular
The distal fragment loses its blood supply, causing necrosis of the trapezium
The median nerve always crosses the fracture line
The scaphoid lies in the distal carpal row and heals poorly

questions.correctOptionText: The proximal fragment has a retrograde blood supply and may become avascular

distractorRationale.b: It is the proximal fragment, not the distal fragment, that is at risk.
distractorRationale.c: Nerve injury is not the main concern in a scaphoid waist fracture.
distractorRationale.d: The scaphoid is in the proximal row.

questions.explanation: Blood enters the scaphoid mainly at its distal part and runs back to the proximal pole, so a waist fracture can leave the proximal fragment without supply, risking avascular necrosis and non-union. Because early X-rays can be normal, the wrist is immobilised and further imaging is arranged.

questions.stem: Which muscle is the strongest supinator of the forearm when the elbow is flexed to 90 degrees?

distractorRationale.c: Brachioradialis acts best with the forearm in mid-position, flexing the elbow.

questions.explanation: Biceps inserts into the radial tuberosity and, when the elbow is flexed, it is well placed to rotate the radius into supination. When the elbow is extended, supinator contributes more.

questions.stem: During a power grip, which muscles hold the wrist in slight extension so that the long finger flexors can work efficiently?

options.text: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, and extensor carpi ulnaris
Flexor carpi radialis and flexor carpi ulnaris

questions.correctOptionText: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, and extensor carpi ulnaris

distractorRationale.b: The pronators rotate the forearm, not the wrist.
distractorRationale.c: Lumbricals and interossei are intrinsic muscles that matter for precision grip.
distractorRationale.d: The wrist flexors would increase wrist flexion and weaken the grip.

questions.explanation: Finger flexors cross the wrist and would flex it as they contract; the wrist extensors counteract this and fix the wrist in extension. This keeps the flexor muscles at an effective length, giving a stronger grip.

questions.stem: True or false: the dorsal interossei adduct the fingers.

distractorRationale.a: The dorsal interossei abduct the fingers (DAB); the palmar interossei adduct them (PAD).

questions.explanation: The dorsal interossei abduct the fingers away from the middle finger, and the palmar interossei adduct them towards it. The mnemonic DAB and PAD gives the pair of actions.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old is lifted by one hand and immediately cries and refuses to use the arm, holding it still beside her body with the forearm pronated. Which is the most likely mechanism?

options.text: Subluxation of the radial head from under the annular ligament

questions.correctOptionText: Subluxation of the radial head from under the annular ligament

distractorRationale.b: Scaphoid fractures follow a fall on the outstretched hand and are uncommon at this age.
distractorRationale.c: Lunate dislocation follows high-energy wrist trauma.
distractorRationale.d: Biceps rupture is unusual in children.

questions.explanation: In young children the radial head is not fully formed and the annular ligament is loose, so traction on the extended pronated arm can pull the head from beneath it. The child then guards the arm, which is typically held in pronation.

questions.stem: Which statement about the intrinsic muscles in precision grip is correct?

options.text: The thenar muscles are supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, while most other intrinsic muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve
All intrinsic muscles of the hand are supplied by the median nerve
The interossei are supplied by the radial nerve
The thenar muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve

questions.correctOptionText: The thenar muscles are supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, while most other intrinsic muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve

distractorRationale.b: The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles and the first two lumbricals only.
distractorRationale.c: The radial nerve supplies extensors, not the intrinsic hand muscles.
distractorRationale.d: The ulnar nerve supplies adductor pollicis and the hypothenar muscles but not the thenar muscles.

questions.explanation: Median nerve lesions at the wrist weaken thumb opposition and abduction (thenar muscles), whereas ulnar nerve lesions weaken finger abduction, adduction and the adductor pollicis. Precision grip needs both.

questions.stem: List the carpal bones in the proximal and distal rows from lateral to medial, and explain why a fracture of the scaphoid waist may lead to avascular necrosis.
markingGuide: Proximal row: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform.
Distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.
Scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, often after a fall on the outstretched hand.
Blood supply enters distally from the radial artery and runs retrograde to the proximal pole.
A waist fracture can cut off supply to the proximal fragment, leading to avascular necrosis or non-union.
questions.explanation: The retrograde blood supply explains why the proximal pole is at risk. Because early radiographs may not show a scaphoid fracture, tenderness in the snuffbox should lead to immobilisation and further imaging.

questions.stem: Compare the power grip and the precision grip in terms of the muscles used and the position of the wrist, and give an everyday example of each.
markingGuide: Power grip: example such as gripping a hammer; fingers flex around the object with the thumb across it.
Long flexors (flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, flexor pollicis longus) provide the force.
Wrist extensors (ECRL, ECRB, ECU) hold the wrist in extension to keep the flexors at an effective length.
Precision grip: example such as holding a pen; uses fingertips and thumb pad.
Intrinsic muscles (lumbricals, interossei, thenar muscles, adductor pollicis) provide fine control.
questions.explanation: Power grip depends on strong extrinsic muscles with the wrist stabilised in extension, whereas precision grip depends on the small intrinsic muscles that control the fingers and thumb. Both rely on the nerves of the forearm and hand being intact.
